content: Covered smut in barley is a disease caused by the fungal pathogen Ustilago hordei. This disease is distributed globally and is more widespread compared to loose smut or false loose smut. Symptoms Plants infected with covered smut do not exhibit visible symptoms until the heading stage. At this point, the kernels of infected plants are replaced by dense masses of dark brown smut spores. The affected heads become hard and compact. Infected plants may also exhibit stunted growth. Occasionally, smut sori can develop on the leaf blades, where they appear as elongated streaks. Disease Cycle The infection is seed-borne, with the fungus penetrating the endosperm during the grain formation process. Seeds that are infected give rise to systemically infected plants. The fungal mycelium advances through the host tissue and establishes itself just behind the growing point of the plant. The spores produced by the fungus are not easily dispersed by wind or rain. During harvest, the spore masses are broken apart, scattering spores onto the grain. In some cases, intact spore masses remain visible in the harvested grain. The fungus survives the winter as teliospores, which persist on seeds or in the soil. Pathotypes At least 13 distinct pathotypes of Ustilago hordei have been identified. The virulence of these pathotypes is controlled by at least three single recessive and independent gene pairs. Management The management of covered smut involves the use of resistant barley cultivars and seed treatments. Fungicides Effective seed treatments for controlling covered smut include fungicides such as carboxin, fenpiclonil, tebuconazole, triadimenol, and triticonazole.
